description: We are a team originally all taught @ IIMAS, UNAM. We are passionate about scientific research and applied methods for solving critical problems the humankind is or might be facing in the upcoming years. Strongly driven by a data mindset covering a wide range of expertise in computer science, data science, physics and statistics.
summary:
We built YoliA: a mobile crop-rotation advisor for Mexican farmers. It has two main tools: a Spanish-language WhatsApp assistant and a phone-friendly web app. In either one, a farmer describes their field, water source and priorities. The tool then compares their current rotation with at least two alternatives and explains why each was suggested, the evidence behind it, likely benefits and information gaps. The web app adds maps and climate scenarios. Both tools run on two engines. One uses WOFOST crop simulations to test how rotations perform under each field’s climate and soil. The other uses observed district-level outcomes from SIAP combined with NASA data (POWER climate trends, MODIS, SMAP soil moisture and GRACE groundwater storage).

Our interviews validation with an agronomist showed that short-term profit and a lack of nearby buyers block rotation changes more than agronomy does, so we weigh market access alongside soil health and water use. Many farmers and extension workers in Mexico have limited access to a computer but already use WhatsApp every day, so we designed everything for the phones they already have. Our tool supports farmer judgment and doesn’t replace it. 

This is a demonstration prototype, not a production-ready platform. Hackathon constraints limit its AI responses and data retrieval. It demonstrates our proposed framework, which we aim to validate with field data and expand into a sustainable service benefiting both farmers and providers.
details:
What it does

YoliA turns NASA Earth observations into practical planting decisions for Mexican agronomists. It is a Spanish-first, mobile web app, also designed to be integrated into WhatsApp, that helps farmers and technicians compare two-year crop rotations before buying seed. A farmer marks their plot on a map and tells YoliA what they planted last season, whether they rely on rain or irrigation, and what matters most: income, water savings or soil health. YoliA shows their current rotation next to at least two alternatives, each explained in plain Spanish: why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, what it could improve and what is still unknown. A guided “Agricultor” mode serves farmers; a “Técnico“ mode shows technicians the numbers behind every answer.

How it works

Two engines power these answers.

1. The first gathers NASA data for the plot (POWER weather, MODIS vegetation and evapotranspiration, GPM rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and SRTM elevation) plus SoilGrids soil properties, and stores it in Google Cloud, where the WOFOST crop model simulates every two-year sequence of maize, wheat, chickpea, sorghum and fallow, rainfed and irrigated, and ranks them by the farmer's priorities.

2. The second engine covers Mexico's 191 SIAP districts, combining 2003–2025 production and price records with NASA GRACE groundwater trends, so alternatives come from crops the district already grows and sells.

Benefits

Farmers compare options before committing a season, seeing income, water use and soil health on one screen.

On an irrigated farm in Sinaloa, adding winter chickpea between two maize seasons could raise two-year gross income from about 87,600 to 144,500 MXN per hectare and lift a soil-diversity index from 17 to 83, though it needs roughly twice the irrigation water.

Every figure shows its source, so technicians can trust and explain it. Our AI assistant makes insights accessible to everyone, offering clear, actionable explanations for non-technical users and in-depth technical analyses for those seeking a deeper understanding.

Intended impact

Our goal is to make rotation planning a normal pre-season step for Mexican smallholders, leading to fewer empty fields, more soil-building legumes and smarter use of scarce water. Next, we'll validate results with local field data.

Tools and technologies

We built YoliA with Python, TypeScript and JavaScript: WOFOST through PCSE on Google Cloud virtual machines and Cloud Storage, a Node.js, React and web app with Leaflet maps, and Twilio for WhatsApp. No special hardware is needed beyond an ordinary smartphone.

What makes it creative

YoliA is creative because it plans rotations, not single crops: soil water carries over between seasons, so the model captures how one crop sets up the next. The same data ranks options differently for a farmer seeking income than for one saving water, and alternatives favor crops the region already sells. Honesty is a feature: gross revenue is never called profit, and missing data is never shown as zero.

Factors we considered

An agronomist we interviewed told us tools fail when they ignore short-term cash flow or suggest crops with no local buyer, so we put income and market access at the center. Since many farmers lack a computer, we designed for phones, plain Spanish and voice input, and the plot's location never leaves the phone. Because the model is not yet calibrated with field data, YoliA doesn't forecast yields: it supports farmer judgment rather than replacing it.
